notes.o1: Today I will present the complete journey through both iterations of the scheduling algorithm research. The goal was to improve daily aircraft availability by changing maintenance timing while preserving the maintenance rules. Iteration 1 established the objective and made the search practical. Iteration 2 tested whether a more exploratory method could improve it, investigated starting schedules, and finished a wider hyperparameter study. I will focus on the measured findings and the final recommendation. The supporting diagrams and earlier plots are available after the references for questions.
notes.o2: The original motivation comes from the Blackhawk deployment example in the seminar. The reported readiness figure looked strong, but nine of the twenty-four aircraft could not deploy because maintenance was too close. The important connection to this project is that average availability alone can hide a concentrated shortage. We therefore care especially about the worst day across the forecast. This example motivates the scheduling problem, rather than defining the operational assumptions of the prototype. Sources: Pippin, Allocating Flight Hours to Army Helicopters, 1998, and the U.S. Army image attribution retained from presentations/Seminar.pptx.
notes.o3: The scheduling problem starts when several aircraft enter maintenance at similar times. Availability then falls even if the average across the year looks acceptable. The decision variable is the start of a check inside its legal start window. Checks must not overlap on one aircraft, and changing one check must preserve the sequence and the reset rules for later checks. The score ranks worst-day availability first, lower population standard deviation second, and mean availability last. A smoother schedule cannot compensate for a lower worst day. Random failures and resource shortages motivate the problem, but the reported experiments model scheduled maintenance. Source: CONTEXT.md and the completed technical report dated 12 October 2026.
notes.o4: The work developed in two iterations. First, a simple ten-aircraft dataset established that local neighbourhood search could reduce maintenance overlap. Scaling to the heavy forecast made candidate evaluation expensive, so the method progressed through random sampling to deterministic priority selection. The second iteration asked whether basin-hopping with tabu polish could escape local optima, how sensitive the result was to the start schedule, and which neighbourhood settings should be retained. The newest study tests the settings on three matched forecasts. This order shows why each change was needed and how the final recommendation follows from the evidence.
notes.o5: The literature review considered mathematical programming, stochastic simulation, and metaheuristic methods. Winata's work on flight and maintenance planning provided the initial direction of simulated annealing with variable neighbourhood search. The practical implementation began with improving neighbourhood search, so we could establish feasibility and understand the objective before introducing random acceptance. That distinction matters when reading the later results: the final candidate is basin-hopping with tabu polish, while classic single-chain simulated annealing is an earlier ablation. Source: the literature slide and references in presentations/Seminar.pptx, including Winata, 2011.
notes.o7: The first proof of concept used ten aircraft with eight checks each. Each check lasted sixty days, and the model constrained maintenance intervals to the supplied window. The flowchart shows the basic search loop: calculate daily availability, score the schedule, generate neighbours by shifting one check, reject infeasible candidates, and keep the best improvement. Larger timing changes came before smaller changes. On the right, the resulting simple-fleet schedule retains at least eight available aircraft, which was the original target. This established the objective and feasibility checks before the heavy maintenance model made the neighbourhood much larger. Source: presentations/Iteration 1.pptx and Iteration 1 Milestones.pptx.
notes.o8: The heavy forecast contains twenty-four aircraft and two hundred and seventy-eight supplied checks over roughly twelve years. It adds A, B, C, and D check types, with different durations and maintenance reset rules. The repeating sequence is shown on the slide. The availability plot makes the central difficulty visible: long checks can overlap and create a sustained dip. In this model, shifting one check can change the due clocks for later checks on the same aircraft. The optimiser therefore needs to rebuild the later schedule rather than treating every start as an independent variable. The displayed table and plot come from the original iteration presentation.
notes.o9: When the same neighbourhood search scaled to the heavy forecast, an iteration could produce over a thousand candidate schedules. Fully copying, checking, and scoring each one was expensive. Sampling two hundred neighbours reduced the work but introduced uncertainty, because the sample could omit a useful improving move. The next change used the structure of the problem: checks covering the worst availability days are the most relevant place to search first. Priority selection therefore concentrates the work deterministically, while widening the search when a worse priority group cannot improve. Source: Iteration 1 milestone slides 5 to 7.
notes.m8: Each check receives a priority equal to the lowest fleet availability during its maintenance interval. A check covering a day with fifteen available aircraft has priority fifteen. Checks then belong to exclusive priority groups. In this illustration, twenty checks touch the worst days, so a pair of timing shifts produces around forty proposals at that first group. The baseline chooses the best improving move within the first group that can improve the score. If none improves, it expands to the next group. After a move, the later checks on that aircraft are rebuilt and availability is updated incrementally. This combines targeted selection with lower evaluation cost. Source: Iteration 1 Milestones.pptx slides 7 and 8.
notes.m9: The historical milestone comparison reported about nine hundred and twenty seconds for full neighbourhood search, four hundred and fifty-one seconds for two hundred random samples, and fifteen point four seconds for priority selection. That is approximately sixty times faster than full search and thirty times faster than the sampled method in that benchmark. The primary result was an improvement from fifteen to eighteen available aircraft on the worst day. These are the historical Iteration 1 measurements. They are not directly comparable with the timings in the new hyperparameter study, which uses a matched scoring window and a verified study driver. Source: Iteration 1 Milestones.pptx slide 9.
notes.o13: The second iteration focused on three questions. Could a method that temporarily accepts a worse schedule improve the tuned hill-climb? How much did the starting schedule affect the result? And which settings worked consistently across the tested forecasts? Operational constraints were part of the earlier plan, but they are outside the scope requested for this final presentation. Maintenance legality remains necessary throughout. I will separate the earlier controlled start-schedule experiment from the new moderate and wide stagger datasets, because those newer datasets change maintenance opening states and are different problem instances. Sources: Iteration 2 execution plan, completed study records, and the final-presentation scope.
notes.o15: The baseline is an improving priority hill-climb. The candidate is basin-hopping with tabu polish, built on the same maintenance neighbourhoods. It first obtains a polished schedule, perturbs it to leave the current local optimum, and uses tabu search to polish the new schedule. Temperature then determines whether to continue from a worse basin. The best-so-far schedule is tracked separately and is the result we return. This is more structured than simply accepting every generated neighbour along one annealing chain. Classic simulated annealing remains an earlier ablation and is not the candidate in the comparison that follows. Source: .scratch/iteration-2/spec.md and the 12 October 2026 completed technical report.
notes.o16: The implemented candidate can temporarily accept a lower worst-day availability at high temperature. That differs from the original execution-plan slide, which always rejected a lower worst day. The tightened fallback keeps that stricter rule and anneals only when worst-day availability is unchanged. Both versions return the best-so-far schedule. The decision comparison holds the input and half-step neighbourhoods fixed. The random candidate runs use seeds one, two, and three, and we report their median with their spread. Adoption requires all seeds to retain eighteen aircraft, at least zero point zero zero five improvement in standard deviation, and median runtime within five minutes. Sources: docs/adr/0001-temperature-may-lower-worst-day.md and .scratch/iteration-2/study-results.json.
notes.o17: On the original decision benchmark, all reported methods retained eighteen aircraft on the worst day. The tuned hill-climb achieved standard deviation about one point three nine two in one hundred and fifteen point six seconds. Basin-hopping improved the median standard deviation by only zero point zero zero one four four, below the required zero point zero zero five. Its median runtime was three hundred and six point three seconds, just over the five-minute limit. Two runs reached the time budget. Tightened acceptance matched the hill-climb quality. The candidate therefore failed both the smoothness threshold and the runtime criterion. These values use the earlier decision-study horizon and must not be compared numerically with the later matched hyperparameter scores. Source: .scratch/iteration-2/study-results.json, decision section.
notes.o19: This earlier experiment changes the opening start schedule for the same original checks and due dates. The three starts are as-loaded, bunched, and spread. All begin at a worst-day availability of fifteen and finish at eighteen with the tuned hill-climb. The as-loaded start finishes smoothest. Basin-hopping adds a small smoothness improvement on each start but takes longer. This supports retaining the as-loaded start for that original instance. It does not show that a more widely staggered fleet is always worse. The new moderate and wide datasets have different maintenance ages and check mixes, so their results answer a different question. Source: .scratch/iteration-2/study-results.json, stagger section.
notes.o22: The completed hyperparameter study crosses fifty-eight neighbourhood and selection settings with three actual input workbooks, giving one hundred and seventy-four matched sweep cases and two hundred and three total run records. All use the same forecast dates, from twenty-first January 2026 to eighteenth January 2038. The aged fleets retain their saved sequence positions and due clocks, and checks already commenced before the benchmark are frozen. Endpoints receive full rule replay and independent daily availability checks. Serial finalist timing repeats follow the parallel sweeps. The original, moderate, and wide inputs are distinct maintenance problem instances. We compare tuning against the default within each one, rather than calling their differing inputs an algorithm gain. Source: docs/reports/2026-10-14-priority-hyperparameter-analysis-three-datasets.docx.
notes.hyper_results: The best measured setting on the original forecast is C57, half steps plus forty-two days. It retains eighteen aircraft and improves smoothness by one point four two percent against the default. Moderate and wide stagger both favour C30, the wide dense ladder. They retain nineteen and twenty aircraft respectively, with smoothness improvements of three point one and four point eight five percent. All listed winners naturally exhausted their improving neighbourhoods. The previous half-step setting reaches only nineteen aircraft on wide stagger, while the default reaches twenty, so it cannot be adopted universally. Serial timings are local-machine medians, and repeated deterministic endpoints agree. Source: the three-forecast report dated 14 October 2026 and .scratch/priority-hyperparameter-analysis/three-dataset-summary.json.
notes.o20: C30 is the shared recommendation among naturally converged configurations that retain each dataset's best measured worst day. Its shift levels range from plus or minus fifty-six down to plus or minus one day, and it retains first-level priority selection. A four-hundred-iteration cap covers the observed convergence counts with room to confirm no further improvement. On the original input, C30 has only zero point five six percent worse smoothness than the dataset winner. C57 is appropriate when that final original-input smoothness improvement matters. The frozen default stays the reference baseline, and future comparisons should challenge the tuned baseline on each input with matched dates and opening states. Source: three-forecast report, shared-settings recommendations.
notes.o18: The original forecast has a useful bound on the primary objective. A D check lasts one hundred and twenty-six days and has a seventy-day early allowance, so each first D check must cover a fixed fifty-six-day interval beginning at its due date. Six of those mandatory intervals overlap in the original fleet. With twenty-four aircraft, no legal schedule can exceed eighteen available aircraft on every day. Our result reaches that bound. For the two stagger inputs, the corresponding upper bound is twenty-one, while the measured results reach nineteen and twenty. Those gaps remain unresolved. These bounds do not prove globally optimal smoothness. Source: the three-forecast report, limits of the evidence section.
notes.o21: The final recommendation is to retain the priority hill-climb. Iteration 1 delivered the major practical improvement: raising original worst-day availability from fifteen to eighteen and reducing search cost. Iteration 2 showed that basin-hopping's small smoothness gain did not justify its runtime in the decision benchmark. The completed three-forecast study now supports C30 as the shared tuning choice, with C57 as the original-input option. The method, input opening state, and scoring window need to stay explicit in future comparisons. The remaining work is broader validation on new fleets and investigation of the unresolved stagger-input gaps. That completes the project journey, and I am happy to take questions.
